one_liner: Single-file betterC D port of a C epoll 'Hello, World!' HTTP responder; matches the gcc -O3 original within 10%.
what_it_does: A 190-line D program (dlang/epoll/app.d) built with LDC in betterC mode, using only libc and Linux epoll. It accepts keep-alive connections, counts \r\n\r\n terminators in each read and answers with that many copies of a fixed 192-byte response. It is a near line-by-line port of the suite's C server (c/epoll/http_epoll.c, itself adapted from frevib's epoll echo server). It exists as the theoretical ceiling that tchaloupka/httpbench measures D frameworks against. It is not a library: there is no parser, router or API.
how_it_is_fast: It uses the same machinery as the C original. prefork.d launches one process per CPU, each with its own SO_REUSEPORT listener. Sockets are non-blocking, multiplexed with epoll (level- or edge-triggered) and set to TCP_NODELAY. A send buffer pre-filled with 512 copies of the response lets a pipelined batch of N requests go out in one send() of N x 192 bytes, with no allocation per request. betterC drops druntime and the GC, so the D binary is libc calls and syscalls, effectively the same program as the C version. The D port also keeps per-client buffers inline in an fd-indexed static array and takes up to 256 events per epoll_wait (C: 128).
when_to_use: As a reference ceiling for epoll servers on your own machine: run it next to a framework to see how much the framework costs over raw syscalls.
As evidence that betterC D compiled with LDC runs syscall-bound event-loop code as fast as gcc -O3 C, with no GC or druntime.
As a starting point for a fixed-reply Linux endpoint (health check, load-balancer probe) where every request gets the same bytes.
To compare level-triggered and edge-triggered epoll: both variants come from one file via --d-version=EdgeTriggered.
when_not_to_use: Any real HTTP service: it parses nothing, has no routing or request bodies, and aborts on a partial request.
Expecting D to beat C: the tables show parity (0.94x to 1.10x in single runs), with D behind at 64 connections and about 3% behind when pipelined.
Non-Linux platforms: it depends on epoll and accept4.
Processes with more than 511 open descriptors: clients live in a 512-slot array indexed by fd and the runner builds with --boundscheck=off, so a higher fd writes out of bounds.
Slow clients or large replies: send()'s return value is ignored, so a short write silently truncates the response stream.

integration.form: source-drop (one D file run as a dub single-file package: dub build --single app.d)
integration.dependencies: none beyond libc and Linux headers via druntime's core.sys bindings (betterC, no Phobos)
integration.min_toolchain: ldc2 1.29.0 as measured (uses ldc.intrinsics.llvm_expect under LDC, a no-op fallback otherwise); C baseline built with gcc -O3, version unstated
integration.platforms: Linux only (epoll, accept4); measured on x86-64 with --mcpu=native
integration.thread_safety: single-threaded process; scales by running one process per CPU (prefork.d) with SO_REUSEPORT
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial: same protocol behaviour and listen port as the C responder for well-formed keep-alive requests, but it hard-codes port 8080 instead of reading it from argv, and it aborts where the C version waits for the rest of a partial request

gotchas: Harness flaw: the port differs from the C original on error paths. On any read that holds no complete request, or ends with a partial one, D hits assert(0), which kills that worker; C keeps buffering. D ignores send()'s return; C exits on a short send. D uses inline 2048-byte buffers in a 512-slot array; C mallocs 4096 bytes per accept (never freed) in a 2048-slot array. prefork.d does not restart dead workers, and runner.d parses only wrk's Non-2xx line, not 'Socket errors'. So a worker crash would show up only as lower RPS, never as an error count.

Harness flaw: each cell is one 30 s wrk run (no -b best-of option) after a 3 s warm-up, against a 2-vCPU KVM guest. With prefork, each process binds its own SO_REUSEPORT socket, so at 2 and 8 connections the kernel's hash decides how connections split across the two workers. That split can differ between the C and D runs, which is enough to explain the 2-client (1.10x) and 8-client (1.06x) leads. The stated test command covers only 8, 64, 128 and 256 connections; the 2-client table's command is not given.

Flags are unmatched: runner.d appends --release -O3 --boundscheck=off --ffast-math --mcpu=native to D's --betterC, while the C Makefile uses plain gcc -Wall -O3. The gcc version is not recorded: the Dockerfile uses unpinned debian:testing build-essential, and the measured service VM ran Ubuntu 22.04.

Toy request counter, shared with the C version (whose comment calls it 'unusable in real servers'): after a \r that does not start \r\n\r\n it skips ahead 5 bytes. A final header line of one or two characters therefore hides the request terminator. That is harmless for wrk's fixed request and wrong for real clients.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: The siblings are deployable servers (the HttpArena entries, nginx-class proxies) or the same author's during io_uring wrapper. This one is a measuring stick, not a server. In the same httpbench tables it edged during raw (PF) and the C io_uring raw server at every connection count (for example 276,433 vs 253,256 and 246,812 req/s at 256), so use it to bound what D on epoll can reach. Use bladebench's Rust and Zig raw-socket rows for the same kind of comparison in those languages.
verified_claims_summary: In tchaloupka/httpbench (2022), wrk 4.1.0 ran in a 14-vCPU KVM guest and the servers in a 2-vCPU KVM guest on a Ryzen 7 3700X host. The LDC 1.29.0 betterC port served 43,752, 93,942, 176,532, 232,039 and 276,433 req/s level-triggered at 2, 8, 64, 128 and 256 connections, against 39,886, 88,906, 187,141, 226,433 and 261,440 for the gcc -O3 C original. With pipeline depth 10 it served 2,075,254 against 2,132,917. Both send identical 192-byte responses (BPS/RPS), and the ratios of 0.94x to 1.10x are parity within single-run noise.
status_note: Abandoned since 2022-05-30 (19 stars, 4 forks, 89 commits, Unlicense, so copyable with no attribution); nothing has been re-measured since ldc2 1.29.0 and kernel 5.15, and it is a benchmark fixture rather than a maintained component.
